title: 1 · I want, I can
intro: We'll build real sentences from two little engine words — no memorising lists. Take your time, say each answer out loud before you reveal it.

steps.teach: "Voglio" = I want. And Italian's plain "to …" form of a verb ends in -are, -ere or -ire. "parlare" = to speak (English "parley"). Stick it straight onto voglio.
"mangiare" = to eat (think of a French "manger", or an English manger — the box an animal eats from).
"Posso" = I can.
To ask a question you change nothing at all — you just lift your voice at the end.
"non" = not. It sits right in front of the verb, like English "I do not" without the "do".
"adesso" = now. Extra words go on the end.
"venire" = to come. There's your -ire ending.

steps.prompt: I don't want to come now

title: 2 · I must — and how to say "it"
intro: One more engine word, and the little trick Italian uses to hook "it" onto a verb.

steps.teach: "Devo" = I must / I have to. Same shape as before: devo + the plain verb.
"andare" = to go.
"fare" = to do, to make. English "manufacture" hides it: made by hand.
steps.prompt: I have to do it — but first, just: I have to do

steps.teach: Now the trick. "lo" = it. On a plain -are/-ere/-ire verb it hooks onto the END, and the final -e drops off: fare + lo = farlo.
"domani" = tomorrow.
"comprare" = to buy (think "comprare" ~ to compare prices… or just: com-PRA-re).
steps.prompt: I don't want to buy it

steps.teach: "vedere" = to see. An -ere verb this time.

title: 3 · I have, I am
intro: The two verbs you'll lean on most — and they're both irregular, so we take them slowly.

steps.teach: "Ho" = I have. Just two letters, and the h is silent — say "oh".
Italian doesn't say "I am hungry", it says "I have hunger". "fame" = hunger.
"sete" = thirst. Same pattern.
"Sono" = I am.
"stanco" = tired.
"pronto" = ready. It's also how Italians answer the phone.
"Ho bisogno di" = I need — literally "I have need of". "aiuto" = help.

steps.prompt: I'm tired, I want to go now

title: 4 · you, he, she, we
intro: So far everything has been "I". Now we change the last letter of the verb and get four more people for free.

steps.teach: Take parlare (to speak), cut off -are, and add the ending for the person: -o = I, -i = you, -a = he/she, -iamo = we. So: parlo, parli, parla, parliamo.

steps.hint: just the -i ending and a question tone

steps.teach: "bene" = well.
The same endings on mangiare: mangio, mangi, mangia, mangiamo.
The engine words are irregular, so learn them as a little song: posso, puoi, può, possiamo.
And: voglio, vuoi, vuole, vogliamo.
"aiutare" = to help. And "mi" = me — it hooks on the end just like lo did.
"Andiamo" — we go, or let's go. It's the whole sentence.

title: 5 · where, what, when, why
intro: Six question words. Once you have these you can get through a day in Italy on your own.

steps.teach: "Dove" = where. "è" = is. Squash them together: dov'è.
"la stazione" — you already derived this one from -tion → -zione.
"Cosa" = what (you'll also hear "che cosa", same thing).

steps.hint: fare is irregular in the we-form: facciamo

steps.teach: "Quando" = when.
"Perché" does double duty: it's both "why" and "because".
steps.prompt: Why don't you want to come?

steps.teach: "Come" = how. "stai" = you are (feeling).
"Quanto" = how much. "costa" = it costs.

title: 6 · the, a, and more than one
intro: Every Italian noun is masculine or feminine. It sounds like a burden; it's mostly just the last letter of the word telling you which word for "the" to use.

steps.teach: Nouns ending in -o are usually masculine and take "il". "libro" = book.
Nouns ending in -a are usually feminine and take "la". "casa" = house.
Before a vowel, both shrink to l'. "amico" = friend.
For "a": un for masculine, una for feminine.
Plurals change the noun's own ending: -o becomes -i, -a becomes -e. And "the" becomes i (masculine) or le (feminine).
Describing words come AFTER the noun, and copy its ending.

title: 7 · I like it — and me, you
intro: Italian doesn't say "I like pizza". It says "pizza is pleasing to me". Turn it around in your head and the whole thing falls into place.

steps.teach: "Mi piace" = to-me it-is-pleasing = I like it. The thing you like comes after.
If the thing you like is plural, the verb goes plural too: "mi piacciono". "i gatti" = the cats.
"ti" = to you.
"Mi chiamo" = I call myself = my name is.

steps.hint: literally: how do you call yourself?

steps.teach: Before a normal verb, mi and ti go in FRONT — it's only the plain -are/-ere/-ire form they hook onto the end of. So both of these are right:
steps.prompt: Can you help me? (mi in front)
steps.hint: and "Puoi aiutarmi?" from lesson 4 means exactly the same

steps.teach: "capisco" = I understand.

title: 8 · What I did yesterday
intro: One past tense covers almost everything in spoken Italian, and it's built exactly like English "I have eaten".

steps.teach: Take "ho" (I have) and add the verb's past form: -are verbs → -ato. mangiare → mangiato.
-ire verbs → -ito. finire = to finish.
-ere verbs → -uto. vedere = to see… though this one's irregular: visto.
"capire" = to understand. "Non ho capito" is the single most useful sentence you own as a beginner.
"ieri" = yesterday.
Ask it by changing ho to hai (you have).
Verbs of going and coming use "sono" instead of "ho" — and then the ending agrees with you: -o if you're male, -a if you're female.
steps.hint: a woman would say: sono andata
